Action values

A state value says how good it is to be somewhere. An action value says how good it is to take one particular action there and then carry on with the policy. Comparing the action values in a state tells you which action to take.

Policy:

Each cell is split into four triangles, one per action. A triangle shows the exact $q_\pi(s, a)$: the expected return from taking that action once, then following the policy. Click any triangle to test it with episodes.

The maths

The action-value function of $\pi$ is the expected return after taking action $a$ in state $s$ and following $\pi$ afterwards:

$$q_\pi(s, a) = \mathbb{E}_\pi\big[G_t \mid S_t = s, A_t = a\big]$$

Compare $v_\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_\pi[G_t \mid S_t = s]$ from Lesson 21. The only difference is that the first action is fixed instead of drawn from $\pi$. Everything after that comes from $\pi$ and the ice.

The episodes above estimate it the same way as before: start in $s$, force $A_0 = a$, follow $\pi$, and average the returns.

$$Q(s, a) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} G^{(i)} \;\longrightarrow\; q_\pi(s, a)$$

There are $|\mathcal{S}| \times |\mathcal{A}|$ action values, here $16 \times 4 = 64$, against 16 state values. The extra numbers buy something: to choose an action you only compare four numbers,

$$\arg\max_a q_\pi(s, a)$$

with no need to know where the ice might send you. A state value alone cannot rank actions without that knowledge (Lesson 25). This is why the control methods from Lesson 51 onwards learn $Q$, not $V$.

Tick "mark the best action": under the random policy, the best action in a cell already points roughly towards 🏁 and away from 🕳️. Lesson 24 uses exactly that.
